item.title: Docker Fixes Critical Two-Year-Old Hub Flaw That Let One User Push Images as Another (2026)
item.description:
A flaw in Docker Hub, the registry where container images are published and downloaded, let one user push, pull, or delete images as another user. Docker fixed the flaw on September 30 and says it found no evidence that anyone exploited it.

The flaw was in the feature that converts a personal account into an organization, Docker said in a security advisory on October 12. Conversion transferred the account's personal access tokens (PATs) to the user designated as the organization's owner. A PAT is used in place of a password in the registry, and the person who created each token can still use it.

The access was limited to the registry. It did not reach the Docker Hub web interface, and it could not be used to change a password, email address, or two-factor settings, or to take over an account.

Docker tracks the flaw as CVE-2026-105445 and rated it critical. The CVE record it published on October 13 gives the flaw a CVSS 4.0 score of 9.4.

The flaw was open from August 26, 2024, until the fix, a little over two years. Docker made the fix on Docker Hub itself, so there is no update to install.

Docker Hub cannot move a repository from one account to another. A user instead converts a personal account into an organization that keeps the same name, and must name an existing account as its owner.

Each personal access token acts as the account that owns it, at a permission level chosen when the token is created. While the flaw was open, conversion changed the owner recorded for each token and left its secret unchanged.

An attacker could abuse this by creating a token on an account they controlled, converting that account into an organization, and naming another user as its owner. The token would then work at the registry as that user.

The named owner was not asked to confirm the change and was not notified, according to Docker and the researchers who reported the flaw. Docker's conversion page has included the sentence "The new owner receives a notification email" since at least August 2024.

Within the token's permission level, a transferred token could pull, push, or delete images in the named owner's repositories and in organizations the owner could access.

Docker rated the flaw critical because that access "includes publishing images under a legitimate name," it said.

In March and April, attackers used stolen publisher credentials to push malicious Trivy images and malicious KICS images to the publishers' own Docker Hub repositories, according to Docker.

Peter Molnar and Krisztian Hozak of mptrdev.com found the flaw and reported it to Docker, which says it deployed the fix less than four hours after receiving their report. They named the flaw GhostPat.

In their technical write-up, the two say they reproduced the flaw twice on consenting test accounts. They logged in to the registry as the target account, created and pushed to a repository in its namespace, pushed to an organization it belonged to, and pulled its private repositories.

What Docker's Review Covered

Docker reviewed every account conversion made while the flaw was open and compared them with registry logs and token records. It looked for any token used under more than one identity and examined every push made with a transferred token, about 304,000 in all.

"We found no evidence that the vulnerability was exploited," the company said.

Every one of those pushes went to a repository belonging to the converted organization or to its named owner, according to Docker. In the large majority of cases, both accounts belonged to the same person or team.

Where it could not confirm that one person controlled both accounts, Docker analyzed the highest-risk public images without running them and found no malware or tampering.

Docker's registry logs show when a token is used, not that it exists, so a transferred token that was never used left no record in the logs. For that reason, Docker treated every token transferred by a conversion while the flaw was open as possibly affected, whether or not it had been used.

The advisory reports results for pushes. It does not say what Docker found for pulls or deletions made with transferred tokens, including pulls from private repositories.

Who Was Notified and What to Check

On October 2, Docker emailed the users whose accounts had received transferred tokens and, separately, the owners of the organizations involved. Each email listed the tokens by description and creation date.

The advisory does not say how many users or tokens that covers, calling the group only a "limited number" of users.

Anyone who did not receive the email was not exposed and has nothing to do, according to Docker.

On October 8, Docker deactivated the transferred tokens it had identified. Tokens that their owners had asked to keep were not deactivated.

Todd Matens, who publishes a Docker Compose linter called compose-lint, wrote in a blog post that he received two emails on October 2. One was sent to him as an organization owner and the other to his user account. He rotated his two CI tokens and checked the signatures on his 42 published images, tracing each to the CI run that built it.

Docker advises users to review their tokens, revoke any they do not recognize or no longer use, and use organization access tokens, not one person's PAT, for automation that belongs to an organization.

These details help with those checks:

  • Open Account settings, then Personal access tokens. The list shows when each token was created and when it was last used.
  • The researchers describe two traces. One is a token you did not create, whatever its name, because whoever creates a token chooses its description. The other is an organization in the account switcher that you do not remember joining.
  • Organization access tokens require a Docker Team or Docker Business subscription. They are managed by an organization owner, a company owner, or a custom role with that permission, and they do not work with Docker Desktop or Image Access Management.
  • Organization owners on those subscriptions can review past pushes in the activity logs, which record pushed tags and can show the token that pushed them. Docker Home, where the logs are viewed, keeps them for 30 days, and older entries are available through the Docker Hub API.

Docker's Documentation Described the Transfer

Docker's own documentation described the token transfer for about 17 of the roughly 25 months the flaw was open. A documentation change on April 22, 2025, added a note to Docker's conversion page. It said that naming a user as organization owner "will ensure any PATs associated with the user's account are transferred to the organization owner."

Docker removed the note on September 30, minutes after the time it gives for the fix. The dates come from the public history of Docker's documentation, which The Hacker News reviewed.

Docker says it now requires consent before a user is named an organization owner and notifies that user when this happens. It also records every change in token ownership and reviews other features that change who owns a credential.

item.title: Anthropic Warns Small AI Models Could Soon Form Self-Propagating IoT Botnets (2026)
item.description:
Small artificial intelligence (AI) models may be months away from developing capabilities to self-replicate on IoT devices like smart ovens and off-brand Android TV boxes, according to a warning from Anthropic.

The frontier AI lab said small AI models could form autonomous, self-propagating worm botnets that are "challenging to shut down," since "there's no centralized point to shut off."

Prior work has demonstrated that AI agents can act like one by scanning their network, executing an exploit, and copying model weights to a target machine across a GPU cluster with an aim to generate tailored attack strategies and use compromised machines as a botnet to run large language models (LLMs) in order to sustain its reasoning and expand in scale.

"Such an 'AI worm' could carry its model weights with it as it reproduces (or re-download them from a public hub), and then run inference directly on compromised hardware," Anthropic said. "Effectively, the weights would become part of the malware payload."

The idea, at a high level, explains how AI models could potentially break into internet-connected devices and use their computing power to run themselves and spread to other devices, without having to rely on expensive data centers all the time. A more powerful model that's too large to fit into a single device could be split into small chunks and run across multiple machines to collectively run it.

A threat actor could build a distributed LLM botnet from poorly secured IoT devices, making it powerful enough to run a capable model. Some of the ways an AI worm could propagate include -

  • Small models that replicate through a compromise of host machines on which they run, also called weight-based replicators. IoT devices make for a lucrative target because of their minimal security controls.
  • Target datacenters and other high-compute targets to set up unmonitored rogue deployments, also classified as frontier replicators or open-weight replicators based on the model used.
  • Steal an AI service provider's API keys or platform credentials to run copies of itself, also called API-based replicators. In this case, the provider could be deceived into thinking it is serving ordinary API requests from a legitimate customer, without realizing that a malicious or self-replicating system is behind them. However, they are also likely to detect more as unusual API usage could trigger security alerts, leading to the credentials being revoked or the accounts getting blocked.
A fleet of 15 Smart TV boxes running distributed inference of Gemma4-26B-A4B.

In its test of 11 open-weights models from Alibaba, DeepSeek, Google, Meta MoonShot AI, OpenAI, and Zhipu AI (aka Z.ai), Anthropic said it found GLM-5.2 to be the only model to propagate Llama3.1-8B reliably to 8/8 nodes running the redroid Android emulator in 4 out of 5 trials.

It also revealed that an AI IoT worm powered by inexpensive Android TV boxes could be a "slow, distributed" system that can produce a meaningful amount of AI computation when a fleet comprising hundreds of thousands of such devices is networked together to run an inference engine.

Alternatively, it could take the form of a potent cyber model capable of breaching data centers at a high pace, or a model that scams people for compute credits.

"We don't yet have a full rogue replicator, but agents are becoming increasingly capable of completing the individual steps in the replication chain (and passing on their adaptations to future copies of themselves)," Anthropic said.

"We expect AI botnets to infect more than IoT devices, and to use weight-based replication as just one strategy in their playbook. AI botnets could also act intelligently to counter defenders, but we haven’t tested this."

item.title: OpenAI Employee Arrested for Allegedly Planting Hidden Recorder in Executive Conference Room (2026)
item.description:
A Saudi national and employee of OpenAI has been arrested for allegedly planting a hidden recording device in an executive conference room at the company's San Francisco offices to covertly record sensitive conversations.

Abdulrahman Alfozan, 35, has been charged with using or endeavoring to use an electronic, mechanical, or other device to intercept oral communications. He was arrested by authorities on October 9, 2026, the U.S. Department of Justice (DoJ) said. Alfozan had been employed at OpenAI since July 2025, working as an engineering lead. He has since been terminated.

According to Alfozan's LinkedIn profile, he graduated from the University of California, Berkeley, with a master's in data science in 2025. He was previously employed at Meta as a senior systems engineer and went on to become the founding engineer at Nash.

"Abdulrahman Alfozan allegedly concealed a covert recording device inside his employer's executive conference room to secretly capture sensitive communications about the company's super intelligence technology," Kash Patel, Director of the U.S. Federal Bureau of Investigation (FBI), said in a statement.

"Protecting American SI [super intelligence] innovation is essential to safeguarding our nation's economic strength and national security, and the FBI views that mission as one of our highest counterintelligence priorities."

According to the complaint, on or around September 30, 2026, OpenAI personnel discovered a surreptitious audio recording device inserted into a USB port on the back of a television in an executive conference room. The device was said to have been concealed in toilet paper and installed sometime around September 28, 2026.

item.title: Microsoft Patches Record 1,413 Flaws, Including Exploited Windows Shell Bug (2026)
item.description:
Microsoft on Tuesday shattered its own Patch Tuesday record by shipping patches for a whopping 1,413 vulnerabilities, including one that it said has come under active exploitation.

These include 1,102 flaws in Windows, 134 in Office, 61 in Developer Tools, 36 in SharePoint Server, and 22 in SQL Server. Of these, more than 670 relate to privilege escalation, followed by over 300 remote code execution flaws and 250 information disclosure flaws. Over 70 flaws are rated Critical in severity.

"Hundreds of CVEs in a single release used to be the exception; now it's the baseline," Dustin Childs, head of Threat Awareness at the Zero Day Initiative (ZDI), said. "Is AI to blame? Partly. It's accelerating bug-hunting on both sides of the fence, so vendors are finding (and fixing) more flaws, and researchers are finding them faster too."

"But AI isn't creating these bugs out of thin air; it's just shortening the time between a vulnerability existing and someone noticing it. The volume isn't the real story anymore. What matters is that discovery is scaling faster than exploitation, so teams that triage by sheer CVE count instead of exploitability are burning cycles on the wrong bugs. Patch what's proven, prioritized, and public, and treat everything else as this month's new normal."

The three vulnerabilities of note are listed below -

  • CVE-2026-96951 (CVSS score: 8.8) - A command injection vulnerability in Windows Shell that allows an unauthorized attacker to bypass a security feature over a network.
  • CVE-2026-108398 (CVSS score: 8.8) - An untrusted search path vulnerability in .NET Framework that allows an authorized attacker to bypass a security feature locally.
  • CVE-2026-92707 (CVSS score: 5.3) - An improperly controlled sequential memory allocation vulnerability in MessagePack-CSharp that allows an unauthorized attacker to deny service over a network.

Microsoft, which credited Fujitsu's Riku Bamba and Yuya Chudo, as well as Anthropic's Benoit Sevens and a researcher named yhw for reporting CVE-2026-96951, said the vulnerability has been exploited in the wild.

"An attacker who successfully exploited the vulnerability could evade Mark of the Web (MOTW) defenses," the Windows-maker said. "In an email or instant message attack scenario, the attacker could send the targeted user a specially crafted file that is designed to exploit the vulnerability."

"In any case an attacker would have no way to force a user to view attacker-controlled content. Instead, an attacker would have to convince a user to take action. For example, an attacker could entice a user to either click a link that directs the user to the attacker's site or send a malicious attachment."

It's unclear how the vulnerability is being exploited in real-world attacks, by whom, and who has been targeted. The U.S. Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency (CISA) has added the flaw to its Known Exploited Vulnerabilities (KEV) catalog, requiring federal agencies to apply the fixes by October 16, 2026.

CVE-2026-108398 has been acknowledged as publicly known at the time of the release of the patches, with Microsoft stating the security flaw could be exploited to bypass Windows Defender Application Control (WDAC) enforcement and run unauthorized applications on target systems.

"An authenticated attacker could place a specially crafted .NET assembly on an affected system and register it for loading by a protected process," Microsoft said. "Successful exploitation could bypass Windows Defender Application Control restrictions and allow the attacker to execute code within the protected process. User interaction is not required."

"This vulnerability is particularly dangerous as a post-compromise attack technique, enabling attackers with existing local access to circumvent security restrictions without user interaction," Mike Walters, president and co-founder of Action1, said. "Successful exploitation could compromise system integrity, expose sensitive business information, weaken endpoint defenses, and disrupt critical operations."

Microsoft attributed the vulnerability discovery to James Forshaw with Google Project Zero, while crediting an anonymous researcher for reporting CVE-2026-92707. The security flaw is the second to be tagged as publicly disclosed.

Patches have also been released for a non-Microsoft CVE (CVE-2026-21413, CVSS score: 9.8), a heap-based buffer overflow impacting Raw Image Extension that could result in remote code execution.

"An attacker could exploit this vulnerability by convincing a user to navigate to a folder containing a specially crafted RAW image file," Microsoft said. "The vulnerability can be triggered when Windows generates a thumbnail or preview; the user does not need to open the file."

The development comes amid continued use of artificial intelligence (AI)-assisted approaches to discover and remediate security vulnerabilities. Last month, Microsoft addressed nearly 1,000 vulnerabilities. According to Satnam Narang, senior staff research engineer at Tenable, more than 4,000 CVEs have been patched by Microsoft this year alone.

"The sheer volume of vulnerabilities in recent Patch Tuesday releases can easily include several examples of potentially concerning vulnerabilities, each of which might have been more remarkable in its own right back when volumes were lower," Adam Barnett, Lead Software Engineer at Rapid7, said.

Along with this month's updates, Redmond has also introduced a new method to help organizations prioritize security updates by grouping related flaws into what it calls "risk cohorts."

"A risk cohort is a group of CVEs that require a similar customer assessment," Microsoft said. "Risk cohorts are a starting point, not a final decision. Customers should continue to review each CVE for active exploitation, severity, attack vector, user interaction, and product-specific guidance."

item.title: Four-Byte Write and Timing Bug Let Researchers Run Code in Windows SmartScreen Enclave (2026)
item.description:
Security researchers ran their own code inside a protected part of Windows that is meant to stay sealed off even when the rest of the computer is taken over.

The protected area is a VBS enclave, an isolated slice of memory the operating system uses to guard secrets, and the one they broke into handles passwords for a Windows anti-phishing feature.

The work was done in a lab as a proof of concept, has not been seen in real attacks, and Microsoft fixed the flaw in its September 8, 2026 update.

The flaw is tracked as CVE-2026-83498. Microsoft rates it an elevation-of-privilege issue, Critical, with a CVSS score of 7.8, and says it has not been exploited and was not publicly known before the fix. Microsoft also says it found the same issue internally. The research, by the security firm Doyensec, was published October 13, more than a month after the patch.

A VBS enclave is a signed library that a normal Windows program loads but cannot read or change once it is running. The Windows hypervisor keeps the enclave's memory in a more trusted world, called VTL1 or Isolated User Mode, that ordinary code in the normal world, VTL0, cannot reach, according to Microsoft.

The design is meant to protect what is inside even if an attacker has already taken over the normal kernel or is running as SYSTEM. Running attacker-chosen code inside that world is what makes this research notable.

The enclave Doyensec attacked is SFAPE.dll, the component behind Enhanced Phishing Protection in Microsoft Defender SmartScreen. That feature watches text you type or paste and warns you if you enter your Windows sign-in password into an unsafe place, such as Notepad or a phishing page.

To do this without exposing the password, Windows intercepts it at login and stores it in hashed form within the enclave, so later inputs can be checked against it. On a Windows 11 system, the program that loads this enclave is lsass.exe, the process that handles sign-in credentials and runs as SYSTEM.

The attack does not work from a distance. It needs a program already running on the machine that loads and calls the enclave; for SFAPE, that's LSASS. Microsoft's own rating says the same: the attack vector is local, and the attacker needs low-level access and no help from the user. In short, this is a way for code that already has a foothold to reach into the more trusted world next to it, not a way in from outside.

Doyensec built the attack from a small mistake and widened it step by step. Calling the enclave's Initialize function a second time makes it write a fixed four-byte error value to an address the calling program controls, and this time it skips the address check the first call performs.

Doyensec is clear that this alone is weak, writing that calling it an arbitrary write "would be a huge overstatement." Aimed at the right spot, though, that one write corrupts the value the enclave uses to tell its own memory from the host's, so its safety check stops working. From there, a timing bug in another function triggers a controlled wipe. That wipe redirects how the enclave looks up a stored object, and the resulting read and write let the researchers replace the table that decides which code the enclave may run.

The result is attacker-chosen code running inside the enclave. The work broke the enclave's isolation; it did not show that a user's password was read or stolen, and Microsoft's advisory describes the impact as data leakage from or code execution inside the enclave.

Microsoft fixed the flaw in the September 8, 2026 cumulative update, KB5124008, for Windows 11 versions 24H2 and 25H2. Doyensec compared the old and new files and found the patched enclave now checks the address before that first write and tightens the function the timing bug relied on.

The update also ships a new policy that prevents the old, vulnerable enclave from loading at all, so a patched system cannot run it. There is no separate workaround to apply; installing the update is the action.

One gap outlives this fix. Windows has no general blocklist for vulnerable enclaves like the one it keeps for vulnerable drivers, and the September policy only blocks the old SFAPE file. An older Microsoft Edge enclave with a similar read-and-write flaw, CVE-2023-36880 from 2023, is still allowed to load, Doyensec said.

Whether that was a deliberate choice or an oversight is unclear. That matters because loading a signed but flawed enclave is a known trick, sometimes called "bring your own vulnerable enclave," that earlier research from Akamai and Outflank used to hide code and data from security tools. Blocking one flawed enclave while leaving another loadable leaves that trick available.

item.title: AI-Found Linux Kernel Flaw Gives Local Users Root, and Can Break a Guest Out to the Host (2026)
item.description:
A flaw in Linux's vhost subsystem lets a local user read and write kernel memory at will and become root across nearly a decade of kernel versions. In one virtualization setup, it lets an untrusted virtual machine write to the host's memory and hijack the program that runs the virtual machine.

The bug is tracked as CVE-2026-74580 and named Vghost. Tencent Zhuque Lab, which found the flaw, released a fix on August 3 and published a full write-up on October 12 with working demos of both attacks. There is no public sign it has been exploited yet.

vhost is the part of the Linux kernel that speeds up network and other input/output for virtual machines and containers. A local user reaches it by opening a device node, usually /dev/vhost-net or /dev/vhost-vsock.

On the host, the flaw gives an unprivileged user a reliable way to read and write any kernel address, bypass KASLR, and escalate to root. The attack is deterministic: it needs no memory grooming and no lucky timing.

The second attack is narrower. When a virtual machine's virtio device is placed behind a virtual IOMMU with iommu_platform turned on, and vhost runs in device-IOTLB mode, an untrusted guest can trigger the same bug and make the host kernel write out of bounds into the host's QEMU process. From there, a guest can overwrite a function pointer in QEMU and take control of where the host process runs next, or crash it.

How it works

vhost keeps a small cache of the memory mappings behind each virtual ring and the shared queues it uses to move data. A cache hit is treated as proof that the region was already checked. The cache is cleared when the mapping is updated or invalidated and when the queue is reset, but not when the VHOST_SET_VRING_ADDR or VHOST_SET_VRING_NUM commands change the ring's addresses or size while the queue is live.

With a device IOTLB attached, those commands accept the new addresses without checking them, leaving that check for later. Once the cache is filled, the subsequent check never runs, and vhost continues translating new addresses using the old mapping. The kernel then copies data to or from that pointer without a bounds check, so a write to the used ring or a read of a descriptor lands outside the mapped region. That gives the attacker kernel read and write.

The flaw sat in the code for about nine years because it took two reasonable changes to create it. A 2017 change (Linux 4.11) added the cache and its shortcut. A 2020 change (Linux 5.9) moved address checking out of the command and into a later step, removing the check that would otherwise have caught the stale translation.

Who is affected, and what to do

The flaw affects Linux kernels from 4.11 up to 7.2-rc4. Tencent reproduced the full local-user-to-root chain on five distribution kernels: Ubuntu 26.04, RHEL 9.8, Amazon Linux 2023, Microsoft Azure Linux 3.0, and Oracle Linux 10.2. On Ubuntu, the device node was limited to the kvm group, so the starting point there was a member of that group rather than any user.

On the other four tested images, the node was world-readable at mode 0666, so any local user could reach it.

The fix (commit de845981da67) clears the cache whenever the ring is reconfigured. Install a kernel that contains it and reboot. The first fixed upstream stable releases are listed below; vendors may also backport the fix without changing their version number.

Stable branch First fixed version
5.10.y 5.10.265
5.15.y 5.15.216
6.1.y 6.1.183
6.6.y 6.6.152
6.12.y 6.12.104
6.18.y 6.18.45
7.1.y 7.1.9
7.2 7.2

Red Hat, Amazon Linux, and Oracle Linux have shipped fixes. Ubuntu has fixed 22.04 and, as of October 13, still lists its 24.04 and 26.04 kernels as in progress.

Until a fixed kernel is in place, restrict access to the vhost device nodes. Remove world access to /dev/vhost-net and /dev/vhost-vsock, limit the owning group to trusted virtualization services, and treat membership in that group as a privilege while the vulnerable kernel is running.

There is no interim workaround for the guest-to-host escape; for that path, the patched kernel is the only remedy.

The severity, and the AI finder

The flaw is rated high, not critical, and the raters disagree on how high. The kernel.org CVE team scores it 8.8 and marks its scope as changed, because the guest-to-host write reaches memory in the host's QEMU process and crosses the boundary between a guest and its host.

Red Hat scores it at 7.3 and marks the scope as unchanged, treating the impact as remaining within the host's own trust boundary; it also rates the integrity impact lower. Amazon scored it 7.8 and Oracle 7.3.

The bug was found with help from Corvus AI, a multi-agent system Tencent built for kernel vulnerability research. The upstream fix credits it with an Assisted-by line, and Tencent says the pipeline found the flaw.

This is machine-assisted research, not an attack run by AI. It is the same team and pipeline behind an 18-year-old SCTP kernel flaw disclosed in August, which also reached root and, in testing, escaped a container.

From there, a guest can overwrite a function pointer in QEMU and take control of where the host process runs next, or crash it.

How it works

vhost keeps a small cache of the memory mappings behind each virtual ring and the shared queues it uses to move data. A cache hit is treated as proof that the region was already checked. The cache is cleared when the mapping is updated or invalidated and when the queue is reset, but not when the VHOST_SET_VRING_ADDR or VHOST_SET_VRING_NUM commands change the ring's addresses or size while the queue is live.

With a device IOTLB attached, those commands accept the new addresses without checking them, leaving that check for later. Once the cache is filled, the subsequent check never runs, and vhost continues translating new addresses using the old mapping. The kernel then copies data to or from that pointer without a bounds check, so a write to the used ring or a read of a descriptor lands outside the mapped region. That gives the attacker kernel read and write.

The flaw sat in the code for about nine years because it took two reasonable changes to create it. A 2017 change (Linux 4.11) added the cache and its shortcut. A 2020 change (Linux 5.9) moved address checking out of the command and into a later step, removing the check that would otherwise have caught the stale translation.

Who is affected, and what to do

The flaw affects Linux kernels from 4.11 up to 7.2-rc4. Tencent reproduced the full local-user-to-root chain on five distribution kernels: Ubuntu 26.04, RHEL 9.8, Amazon Linux 2023, Microsoft Azure Linux 3.0, and Oracle Linux 10.2. On Ubuntu, the device node was limited to the kvm group, so the starting point there was a member of that group rather than any user.

On the other four tested images, the node was world-readable at mode 0666, so any local user could reach it.

The fix (commit de845981da67) clears the cache whenever the ring is reconfigured. Install a kernel that contains it and reboot. The first fixed upstream stable releases are listed below; vendors may also backport the fix without changing their version number.

Stable branch First fixed version
5.10.y 5.10.265
5.15.y 5.15.216
6.1.y 6.1.183
6.6.y 6.6.152
6.12.y 6.12.104
6.18.y 6.18.45
7.1.y 7.1.9
7.2 7.2

Red Hat, Amazon Linux, and Oracle Linux have shipped fixes. Ubuntu has fixed 22.04 and, as of October 13, still lists its 24.04 and 26.04 kernels as in progress.

Until a fixed kernel is in place, restrict access to the vhost device nodes. Remove world access to /dev/vhost-net and /dev/vhost-vsock, limit the owning group to trusted virtualization services, and treat membership in that group as a privilege while the vulnerable kernel is running.

There is no interim workaround for the guest-to-host escape; for that path, the patched kernel is the only remedy.

The severity, and the AI finder

The flaw is rated high, not critical, and the raters disagree on how high. The kernel.org CVE team scores it 8.8 and marks its scope as changed, because the guest-to-host write reaches memory in the host's QEMU process and crosses the boundary between a guest and its host.

The bug was found with help from Corvus AI, a multi-agent system Tencent built for kernel vulnerability research. The upstream fix credits it with an Assisted-by line, and Tencent says the pipeline found the flaw.

This is machine-assisted research, not an attack run by AI. It is the same team and pipeline behind an 18-year-old SCTP kernel flaw disclosed in August, which also reached root and, in testing, escaped a container.

item.title: An AI Agent Found a Critical OTP Bypass in Production. The Attack Was the Easy Part. (2026)
item.description:
The bug was simple: the login let you choose where your sign-in code went. Proving it on a live website was the hard part.

TL;DR

  • During an authorized assessment, an AI pentesting agent found a critical authentication bypass on a major insurer's production website, on its own.
  • One login request let the user choose where the one-time passcode went.
  • The attack was the easy part. Proving it on a live site took web context built over a decade.

The Login Worked. Then the Agent Stopped.

Reflectiz's AI pentesting agent was mapping the login flow of a major insurer's production website, which has millions of users.

The agent requested a login code and directed it to an email inbox it controlled. The code arrived. The login went through. Its guardrails halted the test after the login succeeded. 

The agent had discovered a critical-severity authentication bypass on its own. Reflectiz reported it to the insurer.

The Flaw: The Request Chose Where the Code Went

A one-time passcode (OTP) only proves who you are if it goes somewhere already linked to the account. Here, that link was broken.

The login request carried two fields that decided delivery: the channel and the address. Normally, the code went by text to the phone number on the account. But the request could change the channel. Switch it to email, and the server sent the code to whatever address the request named, not the address registered to the account.

Simplified, the request looked like this:

The server never checked that the address belonged to the account.

Binding a code to its account is one of the most basic checks in authentication. OWASP's testing guide asks this in plain words: "Are the OTPs tied to the correct user account...?"

An attacker with the required customer identifiers could potentially use the flaw to access that customer's account.

From a Suspicious Field to a Proven Bypass

The agent began with reconnaissance, looking at the site's JavaScript and the API calls behind its pages. That analysis surfaced the OTP request and two values that appeared to control how and where the code was sent. Values like those can suggest a hypothesis, but they’re not a finding, since the server might reject the changes or block them later in the login. So the agent built a targeted test around both values and ran it through the live login flow, which confirmed the bypass.

Illustration of the authenticated state the agent reached before stopping. Recreated and anonymized.

Web Context Is the Hard Part

Plenty of automated testing stops at the login gate, but much of what matters sits behind it. A testing system that cannot reach a workflow cannot assess what happens inside it.

Reflectiz solved that problem long before the agent existed. The company has spent more than a decade scanning thousands of production websites, which meant logging in, receiving verification codes, and navigating multi-step flows. So, on sites the company already monitors, the agent starts with that context instead of a blank URL.

Reflectiz's agentic pentesting puts that web context to work. It drives a real browser through the flows a customer follows, including one-time passcodes and 2FA.

Reflectiz CTO and co-founder Ysrael Gurt, a longtime ethical hacker, built the agent on that foundation. 

One Finding Is Not a Coverage Report

A confirmed vulnerability may show what failed, but it doesn’t show how much of the application was tested.

The OTP test ran alongside other attack plans on the same site. Reflectiz's agentic pentesting pairs that open-ended investigation with a structured plan: test every discovered endpoint against every applicable attack category. A separate validator agent reproduces each suspected finding with the same payload and context before it is reported.

The output is a coverage record of which tests ran, their recorded outcomes, and any exclusions.

Pentested Is Not the Same as Secure

The insurer said it had pentested the site about six months earlier. This assessment found an exploitable login flaw, though it is unclear when the weakness was introduced.

That is not a reflection on human testers, because a skilled tester could have found this flaw too. It’s more a reflection on the nature of point-in-time testing. It has its place, but how often can anyone afford to look?

Websites change with every release, but pentest schedules don't. They’re rigid, which isn’t much use against attackers who now use AI to find flaws fast and won’t wait for the next test window. 

Agentic testing keeps pace. It can repeat focused tests as often as the site changes, provided the agent has the right access and clear boundaries, and produces evidence a reviewer can verify.

Reflectiz reports up to 10x the testing capacity at the same operational cost as traditional manual pentesting. The comparison concerns testing volume, rather than a guarantee of 10x more vulnerabilities found. item.title: Hirudo Android Trojan Uses Patched Banking Apps to Bypass Their Built-In Security Checks (2026)
item.description:
Cybersecurity researchers have disclosed details of a new Android banking trojan called Hirudo that works by replacing legitimate banking apps with purpose-built patched versions designed to bypass security checks from inside the app itself, marking a new escalation in financial fraud. 

Dutch mobile security company ThreatFabric said it identified replacements for eight Indonesian banking apps, while credential targeting in the malware spans Indonesia, China, India, Mexico, Morocco and Thailand.

"The operation combines credential theft, device takeover, screen and camera capture, and SMS theft, in combination with a fairly mature backend," Eward Driehuis, vice president of fraud engineering at ThreatFabric, said in a statement shared with The Hacker News.

Hirudo facilitates on-device credential theft and live remote control. The malware is delivered by shopping, adult video, and entertainment dropper apps that carry the trojan as a separate installation package, which is then served as an in-app update.

Some of the dropper apps are listed below -

  • Shopora (com.agbbh.kjdrttt)
  • 1V1 X (com.onev.vip)
  • KoiShort (com.koishort.app)
  • ZoyaTV (com.zoyatv.app)

"The lure is functional, loading real content in a WebView, a storefront, a video catalogue or short dramas, so the experience looks legitimate," ThreatFabric explained. "Behind that content the dropper runs a fixed startup routine: it collects promotion-tracking data, fetches its campaign configuration, and checks whether the payload, the Hirudo RAT, is already installed with its accessibility service and notification access enabled."

If it's not present, it displays a fake in-app update prompt to trigger the installation of the malware. It's worth emphasizing that Hirudo is installed as a second app and must be granted its own permissions before it can carry out the malicious activities.

As observed in the case of StreamRat, the malware implements an anti-detection technique based on blocking Internet access by configuring a deliberately non-functional VPN connection prior to the payload installation. This is seen as an attempt to prevent other apps and services, like Google Play Protect, from carrying out cloud-based checks of the payload.

"However, Play Protect also provides offline detection for known potentially harmful applications, meaning that the mechanism does not completely disable its protection," ThreatFabric noted last month. "We therefore assess that the technique is more likely intended to reduce the effectiveness of online reputation and code-analysis mechanisms rather than bypass Play Protect entirely."

Depending on the nature of the lure app used, the dropper is also designed to serve bogus screens to capture payment PINs, serve fake screens requesting login credentials for banks and wallet apps, display fake lock screen pattern and PIN overlays, and facilitate total remote control of the device.

While all this behavior is par for the course when it comes to Android banking trojans, it's their attempts to replace the target banking app with a tampered copy that stand out. Specifically, the purpose-built replacements embed a hooking engine to blind signature, accessibility, screen-capture, and Play Integrity checks from within the app. The replacement targets eight Indonesian apps.

"For these, the RAT detects the installed banking app through accessibility, checks its signing certificate against a stored reference, [and] then shows a fake 'update' prompt," ThreatFabric explained. "It opens Android's uninstaller for the genuine app without waiting for the user to tap, and downloads the bank-specific replacement in parallel."

While the need for having to remove the app before installing its near-identical malicious copy is a "real constraint," the mechanism offers the ability to bypass the banking app's own security checks by returning responses fed by the attacker beforehand.

This involves returning the genuine app signing certificate, returning an empty list when querying for enabled accessibility services, and stripping the FLAG_SECURE flag so that the app's screens can be viewed and recorded remotely.

"Key-attestation certificates are re-signed with a bundled keybox, and Play Integrity requests are relayed over plain HTTP to an operator-controlled server, which returns a verdict for the app to accept," the mobile security company said.

"Two details are worth underlining for defenders. First, the attestation keybox the engine ships is not the operators' own: it is a publicly leaked keybox. Second, because the Integrity request is relayed rather than genuinely produced, a valid Integrity response alone is not evidence of an untampered app."

Evidence indicates that the malware is distributed via fake web pages masquerading as Google Play Store landing pages for shopping, short drama, and football apps. Unsuspecting users are assessed to be directed to these websites through ads on Meta-owned social media platforms.

The entire operation rests on a backend that combines device control with the ability to manage different campaigns and stolen data, including device records, lock-screen history, and financial profiles containing monthly income and risk-score fields.

"Hirudo marks a deliberate escalation in how Android bankers approach hardened applications," ThreatFabric said. "By moving its tampering inside the target app, the operation shifts the contest from the device to the application's own integrity checks, and from a bespoke patch to a reusable engine that can be retargeted at other apps and regions."

"Once an app can be replaced, its locally produced signals, signature, accessibility list, and integrity verdict, must be treated as attacker-influenced and verified server-side," ThreatFabric said.

Last month, the findings came a little over a month after the cybersecurity firm revealed StreamRat's targeting of Spanish-speaking users via Meta and TikTok advertisements impersonating a free TV streaming service named Streamtv Esp to enable control over compromised Android devices.

"StreamRat abuses accessibility services and MediaProjection to provide operators with near-complete control over infected devices, combining VNC and hidden-screen control, UI-tree collection, keylogging, credential-stealing overlays, internet and screen-blocking capabilities," ThreatFabric said.

item.title: Researchers Used a Public OpenAI Model to Build a $250,000 Chrome Full-Chain Exploit in Six Days (2026)
item.description:
A team at security firm XBOW chained three then-unknown Google Chrome bugs into a single attack that runs code on a Windows computer when the user only loads a web page, the company said.

Its researchers built the attack in six days by directing AI agents running OpenAI's publicly available GPT-5.6 Sol model. Google has since confirmed all three bugs, fixed them, and paid XBOW its top $250,000 reward for a full Chrome exploit.

The attack is a full chain: a set of bugs used together to break every layer of Chrome's protection, from a web page all the way to the computer.

Chrome runs web page code inside two nested sandboxes, the barriers that stop a hacked page from reaching the rest of the machine. The chain crossed both. The result was code running outside Chrome on Windows, with no need for the user to click or download anything.

All three bugs are now fixed, and XBOW says they were never used against Chrome users. The two that carry public identifiers were fixed in Chrome 152.0.7977.65 on August 25 and 152.0.7977.82 on September 3.

Chrome updates on its own, but the fix only takes effect after the browser restarts, so the action is to relaunch Chrome and confirm the version is 152.0.7977.82 or later.

The six days are the headline, and they need their frame. XBOW built the awarded chain between Sunday, August 2, and Friday, August 7, during the Black Hat and DEF CON conferences in Las Vegas. That sprint followed months of earlier work: the company set the challenge at a January staff meeting in Malta, and its first full Chrome chain took two months to complete.

One version of the awarded chain nearly failed when a bug it relied on turned out to be one Google already knew about. XBOW had built the exploit in swappable parts with backups ready, so it replaced that part and the chain held. By the company's own count of its usage logs, the six-day run cost about $40,000 in AI charges.

XBOW also drew a line between what the AI did and what people did. The AI agents searched Chrome's source code, tested ideas, built proofs of concept, and wrote the first drafts of the exploit. The researchers chose the targets, supplied context, challenged the agents' results, and decided which pieces to join.

One researcher, Brendan Dolan-Gavitt, built the awarded chain with the agents. "Pre-LLMs a Chrome full chain would take a team of four around 6-9 months to be produced, our first submission took 2 months. The awarded one? six days," Dolan-Gavitt wrote.

The three bugs each sat in a different part of Chrome. Google's own release notes credit Dolan-Gavitt of XBOW for two of them and list the version that fixed each.

Stage Where CVE Fixed in
1 V8, Chrome's JavaScript engine CVE-2026-85045 152.0.7977.82 (Sep 3)
2 Animated-WebP image decoder No public identifier listed Chrome 152 cycle
3 Crashpad, Chrome's crash handler CVE-2026-78952 152.0.7977.65 (Aug 25)
  • The first bug gave the attacker control of memory inside Chrome's JavaScript engine.
  • The second, in the code that reads animated WebP images, used that control to break out of the engine's inner sandbox and make one precise write to the computer's memory.
  • The third, in Crashpad, Chrome's crash handler, which runs outside the sandbox, turned that single write into full code execution on the machine.

Both identified bugs are rated high severity and need the user to load a page. The WebP bug was fixed in the same Chrome 152 cycle, but no public identifier can be confirmed for it: the one XBOW's announcement gives the WebP stage, CVE-2026-85045, is the identifier Google and XBOW's own technical write-up both assign to the V8 bug.

Google's Chrome Vulnerability Reward Program pays up to $250,000 for a full-chain exploit, the most it offers for a single report, under rules it updated in 2026. It awards at most four of these a year. XBOW calls this the first full-chain Chrome reward under the 2026 rules and the first to an autonomous security company.

Before the fixes shipped, the bugs put an estimated 1 billion people running Chrome on Windows at risk of this kind of attack, according to the company.

XBOW's point is the speed. "It only took an estimated $40,000 of compute and six days for a single researcher to produce a chain that previously would have taken months," founder Oege de Moor said in the announcement.

Dolan-Gavitt put the warning for defenders plainly: "Six days and $40k is not a lot of time or money when the payoff is a Chrome chain!" The bar, he wrote, is now much lower. "Defend accordingly."

item.title: How to Run a Deepfake Readiness Drill Before a Cloned Voice Calls Your Team (2026)
item.description:
Cloned voices and synthetic video calls now show up in payment fraud, help desk resets, and access requests. A structured drill shows security teams exactly where verification breaks down, while nothing is at stake.

The call comes in at 4:40 on a Friday. It's the CFO, or it sounds exactly like her, asking the controller to push a supplier payment out before the weekend because a deal closes Monday. She's traveling, she's rushed, and she apologizes for the bad connection. Ten minutes later an email lands with the wire details.

A couple of years ago that scenario was a conference talk. Now it shows up in incident reports. In a 2025 Gartner survey of 302 cybersecurity leaders, 62% said their organization had experienced at least one deepfake attack in the prior 12 months. In the same survey, 43% reported at least one deepfake audio call incident and 37% had run into deepfakes on video calls.

And the wire is only the obvious ask. The same cloned voice can call the help desk to move an MFA token, or ask an identity admin to set up a new global admin ahead of an "audit." A fraudulent wire tends to surface at reconciliation. A quietly added admin account can sit there for months.

Most organizations have a policy that says to verify unusual payment and access requests. Far fewer have checked whether that policy survives a phone call from someone who sounds like the person who signs off on everyone's paycheck. A deepfake readiness drill is how you find out, on your own schedule, with nothing real on the line.

Why detection by ear falls short

Security awareness training has long taught employees to look for tells. Awkward phrasing, an odd sender address, a link that doesn't match the text. Voice clones and real-time face swaps leave fewer of those tells every quarter. Asking people to hear the fake is asking a lot.

In a May 2025 warning about AI-generated voice messages impersonating senior US officials, the FBI noted that cloned voices can sound nearly identical to the real person and told recipients to confirm identity by calling an independently sourced phone number before acting on anything.

Security leaders already know this. In a January 2026 Osterman Research study of 128 US security and IT leaders, commissioned by IRONSCALES, 60% said they lacked confidence in their ability to counter deepfake attacks even with the training they already run.

So the defense has to rest on process more than perception. If an employee runs the same verification step every time money, credentials, or permissions are involved, the quality of the fake stops mattering much. A drill tests whether that step actually happens when someone senior is leaning on them.

Step 1. Map the voices worth cloning and the people worth calling

Start with two short lists.

The first is the people an attacker would impersonate. That means executives who can approve payments or direct staff (CEO, CFO, CIO, CISO, general counsel). Then go a level down. VPs and directors in finance, IT, and HR make requests like these every week, so a call from one of them raises fewer eyebrows than a surprise call from the CEO. Add a few outside contacts with real authority over money or access, like a key supplier's accounts receivable lead or the engineer at your managed service provider.

The second is the people an attacker would call. Accounts payable, treasury, payroll, HR, executive assistants, the IT help desk, and anyone who can grant or change access in your identity platform. The help desk and the identity admins get left off these lists a lot. They shouldn't be. A cloned voice asking for an MFA reset is a fast route to Account Takeover (ATO). A cloned voice asking for a new admin account skips a few steps.

For everyone on the first list, note how much public audio and video exists. Earnings calls, podcast appearances, conference keynotes, webinar recordings, and social media clips all give an attacker training material. A CFO with three hours of recorded keynotes is a much easier clone than one who's never been on camera. It doesn't take three hours, though. A few minutes from a single webinar can be enough, which puts most directors on the list too.

What comes out of this step is a short matrix: the identities most worth faking and the people most likely to get their calls. In most organizations that's a few dozen people. Manageable.

Step 2. Write the verification rules before testing them

A drill without a clear rule only measures instinct. Before running any scenario, document what employees are supposed to do. Strong verification rules tend to share a few traits.

  • Out-of-band callback. Any request to move money, change bank details, share credentials, reset MFA, or change who has access to what gets confirmed through a number pulled from the internal directory or vendor master file. Never a number supplied in the request itself.
  • Clear thresholds. Spell out which actions always require verification, no matter who's asking or how urgent it sounds.
  • Dual approval. Two people sign off on new payees, changed banking details, new privileged accounts, and role changes.
  • Challenge phrases. The most-impersonated executives and their direct support staff share a phrase that rotates on a schedule.
  • No-blame reporting. Anyone who realizes they already acted on a suspicious request (paid it, reset it, granted it) reports it right away, and nobody gets shamed for it. Shame the first person who comes forward and the next one with that sinking feeling keeps quiet while the attacker keeps working.
  • Explicit permission to pause. The CEO and CFO tell their teams, in writing, that nobody gets in trouble for hanging up and calling back.

Don't skip that last one. Deepfake fraud runs on urgency and hierarchy. An employee who thinks slowing down a VP will cost them at review time is the easiest target in the building. So tell people to trust their gut. The voice can be perfect and the request can still feel wrong, and that feeling is worth listening to even when they can't explain it. My advice to every team I talk to: don't just do something, stand there. A minute of standing still and one callback costs nothing. Acting on the fake costs a lot more.

Step 3. Design multi-channel scenarios

Real attacks rarely show up as a single phone call. They usually start in email or chat to set up context, then move to voice or video to apply pressure. Drill scenarios should follow the same path.

Before building anything, get sign-off from legal, HR, and every executive whose identity will be used. Cloning someone's voice without consent creates its own set of problems. Many teams use a consenting executive's voice, a clearly labeled synthetic stand-in, or a live actor working from a script.

Four starter scenarios cover most of the risk.

  1. Urgent wire from the CFO. A spoofed email flags a confidential acquisition payment, followed by a voicemail in the CFO's voice asking the controller to process it before end of day.
  2. Supplier bank change. A message from a known vendor contact announces new banking details, followed by a Microsoft Teams call from the "vendor" to confirm the update.
  3. Help desk reset. A caller who sounds exactly like the VP of sales says she's traveling, locked out, and needs MFA moved to a new phone before a board meeting.
  4. Access cleanup. An email from the CISO's office announces a quarterly permissions review. Then a Teams call from the "IT director" walks an identity admin through it. Strip excess rights from five users who don't need them, and while you're in there, add a contractor account to a privileged group for the auditors. The cleanup is good hygiene. The one addition is the attack.

Time the scenarios around the same pressure points attackers pick. Quarter close, audit season, the days before a holiday, and weeks when executives are publicly known to be on the road.

Step 4. Run it in stages

Start with a tabletop exercise. Walk the target group through each scenario in a conference room and ask what they'd do at every step. It surfaces policy gaps cheaply. (Someone almost always asks which number they're supposed to call, and nobody in the room is sure.)

Then move to live simulations with a small group. A few ground rules keep it safe.

  • Brief a small control group. The executive sponsor, the SOC lead, and the head of finance should know the drill is running so a real escalation doesn't kick off a real incident response.
  • Keep money and access out of reach. Use a test payee, a payment request that stops at approval, and a sandbox group with no real privileges. Nothing real should be able to move.
  • Set stop conditions. If a participant gets distressed or the scenario starts bleeding into real business, end it and debrief on the spot.
  • Tell participants afterward, every time. A drill that feels like a trap burns the trust the whole program depends on.

Step 5. Measure what actually happened

A single pass/fail score is the least useful number a drill produces. The behaviors underneath it tell security teams far more.

  • Verification rate. The share of participants who used the documented callback or challenge step before acting.
  • Time to escalation. How long it took someone to report the request to security, if anyone did.
  • Report path. Whether the report reached the SOC through the expected channel or stalled in a manager's inbox.
  • Break points. The exact step where the process failed. No directory number, an unclear threshold, or the "executive" pushing to skip the callback.
  • Bundled requests. In the access scenario, whether anyone questioned the privilege grant tucked inside the cleanup, or approved the whole batch because most of it looked right.
  • Trust signals cited. What participants say convinced them. "It sounded exactly like him" and "the email came first, so I assumed it was real" point to very different fixes.

Spend the most time on the break points. Each one maps to a specific fix in policy, tooling, or training.

Step 6. Debrief, fix, and repeat

Keep debriefs blameless and fast, ideally the same day. Most people who fall for a good drill feel lousy about it. Tell them it was built to fool them, because it was. Then walk participants through what was fake, how it was built, and which signals they could have checked. Fix what broke. Update the callback directory, tighten thresholds, and fold the scenarios into the regular phishing simulation program so the lessons don't fade after one round.

Repeat the drill at least twice a year, and any time the high-exposure list changes. A new CFO, an acquisition, or a heavy conference season all count. Rotate scenarios so nobody passes by recognizing the script.

Where technology fits

Process carries most of the load. Tooling helps at two points in the attack chain.

The first is the setup message. Most voice and video deepfake attempts are preceded by an email or chat message that establishes context. Behavioral email security that flags unusual requests from executives, managers, or vendor contacts can break the chain before the call ever happens.

The second is the call itself. Real-time identity verification for collaboration platforms like Microsoft Teams analyzes voice and video during a meeting and warns participants when someone doesn't match the identity they claim. Many detection tools look for artifacts, the glitches a generator leaves behind, and those get harder to spot with every model release. A sturdier approach checks the person, comparing behavioral and biometric signals against a profile of the real speaker. When evaluating these tools, look closely at privacy, specifically whether they record or transcribe meetings or only process signals in the moment. IRONSCALES, the first and only email security platform with deepfake protection built into the product, takes the behavioral and biometric route for Microsoft Teams meetings. It works from mathematical voice and face profiles, with no recordings or transcripts kept.

Start small, start this quarter

A first drill doesn't need a budget line. Two lists, one page of verification rules, four scenarios, and a debrief template are enough to learn where you actually stand.

For finance and compliance teams that want more detail on warning signs, FinCEN's alert on deepfake fraud schemes describes criminals using generative AI to impersonate executives and direct employees to transfer funds. One of its red flags is worth building straight into the drill. Watch for anyone who switches communication methods mid-conversation and blames technical glitches. That "bad connection" from the CFO on a Friday afternoon is exactly the moment to hang up and call back.

Note: This article has been expertly written and contributed by Audian Paxson, Principal Technical Strategist, IRONSCALES.

item.title: curl Patches HTTP/2 Upload Flaw After PoC Demonstrates Client-Side Code Execution (2026)
item.description:
A flaw in how curl handles HTTP/2 uploads lets a malicious server receiving an upload corrupt the client's memory, and the researcher who reported it turned that into code execution on the uploading machine.

The curl project fixed it on October 14 in curl 8.23.0. Taking over a client needs exact knowledge of its build and memory layout, and curl expects a real attack to end in a crash instead.

The flaw, a use-after-free tracked as CVE-2026-92392, affects curl and libcurl 8.12.0 through 8.22.0, both the command-line tool and the library that many other programs use for transfers. curl rates it High on its own four-level scale, its first High-severity flaw since the SOCKS5 heap overflow of October 2023. The project cut its release cycle by two weeks to ship the fix.

The attack runs from the server side. The client has to upload a file of roughly 135KB over HTTP/2 to a server controlled by the attacker, and the server's certificate must pass the client's checks. libcurl negotiates HTTP/2 by default for https:// URLs when the server offers it, and the library was built with HTTP/2 support.

The flaw has shipped in every curl release since 8.12.0 in February 2025. No source reports attacks that use it. The reporter's HackerOne write-up, with the malicious server script and a Docker container described as reproducing the code execution, became public on October 14 with the advisory.

What to Install, and What to Do Until Then

Upgrade to 8.23.0 or apply the fix commit to a local build. curl's machine-readable advisory also lists fixed versions on three older branches, and the project said it would ship updated Rock-solid curl releases, its long-term-support line for customers with support contracts, in step with 8.23.0:

  • curl and libcurl 8.12.0 through 8.22.0: upgrade to 8.23.0
  • 8.14.x branch: 8.14.3
  • 8.16.x branch: 8.16.2
  • 8.20.x branch: 8.20.2
  • Debian 13 (trixie): 8.14.1-2+deb13u7 through DSA-6558-1, per Debian's tracker. Debian 12 (bookworm) does not carry the vulnerable code.

The release fixes 24 CVEs in all. The other 23 are rated Low.

If you cannot update yet, curl's advice is not to use HTTP/2. The --http1.1 option asks the tool for HTTP/1.1, and applications set CURLOPT_HTTP_VERSION to CURL_HTTP_VERSION_1_1. curl's documentation calls that setting a request, because an existing connection on another version may be reused.

HTTP/2 support in libcurl is a build option. A build without it cannot negotiate HTTP/2, so it cannot reach the upload path the advisory describes.

How a Hostile Server Turns the Bug Into Code Execution

Daniel Stenberg, curl's lead developer, explained the bug in a post published with the release, and the public report lays out the code path. HTTP/2 carries several transfers over one connection, and libcurl tracks each transfer with an object it calls an easy handle.

During an upload, the server stalls the transfer by setting the HTTP/2 window to zero, returning part of the response, and then resetting the stream while keeping the connection open. curl treats the reset as a reason to retry.

In cleanup, curl first tells the HTTP/2 layer that the transfer is finished, then flushes the rest of the unsent upload into the same connection. With no transfer registered, those leftover bytes are read as a new request. The line pattern the reporter includes in the uploaded file makes them look like request lines. When they do, a new stream is opened that stores a pointer to the easy handle.

The retry completes on a new HTTP/1.1 connection, and the application frees the handle. The old connection still holds the pointer and uses it when the server sends a frame on that stream, which can happen as the program exits.

In the reporter's exploit, data the server sends lands in the memory the freed handle had used. A request that goes out leaks local addresses, which the server needs to defeat address space layout randomization (ASLR). A function pointer in that memory is overwritten with bytes from the server, and curl then calls it.

Code execution needs the attacker to know the target's exact curl version, architecture, libc allocator and heap layout, to keep two parallel transfers on the right timing, and to fit the payload into about 23 bytes, according to curl's advisory. "The most likely outcome of an attempted attack is rather just a crash," Stenberg wrote, putting the chance of success as slim. That is why curl graded the flaw High rather than Critical.

curl uses four severity levels and publishes no CVSS score. The National Vulnerability Database had not analyzed the record as of October 14.

The fix is a six-line reorder in lib/multi.c by Stefan Eissing. The HTTP/2 layer now gives up its references to the handle after the leftover upload data has been flushed, not before.

The report reached curl on September 15 through HackerOne, and the security team confirmed it within hours, according to Stenberg. On October 7, the project pre-announced a High-severity fix for the next release, shortening its cycle from eight weeks to six.

curl credits the finding to "Luna with Claude, Anthropic." Stenberg names the reporter as Luna Tong of Anthropic, says the finding came through the company's new OSS Scanner, and presumes its AI models were involved.

Anthropic opened OSS Scanner on October 8 as an opt-in service that scans enrolled open-source projects with its models and emails the results without human review, each report with a reproducer and, where available, a candidate patch. The curl report came three weeks before that public launch. Anthropic's launch post quoted Stenberg saying the scanner had turned up "one of the worst curl vulnerabilities reported in the last few years," without naming one.

The same maintainer wrote in July 2025 that about a fifth of curl's security submissions that year were what he called AI slop, and that only about one in twenty had proved genuine.

curl has spent several years reducing the number of internal pointers to handles in favor of identifiers it looks up when needed, Stenberg wrote, and that is no guarantee against another use-after-free. curl calls the bug a mistake that a memory-safe language would likely have avoided, and the project does not plan to rewrite curl in one.

The project cut its release cycle by two weeks to ship the fix.

The attack runs from the server side. The client has to upload a file of roughly 135KB over HTTP/2 to a server controlled by the attacker, and the server's certificate must pass the client's checks. libcurl negotiates HTTP/2 by default for https:// URLs when the server offers it, and the library was built with HTTP/2 support.

The flaw has shipped in every curl release since 8.12.0 in February 2025. No source reports attacks that use it. The reporter's HackerOne write-up, with the malicious server script and a Docker container described as reproducing the code execution, became public on October 14 with the advisory.

What to Install, and What to Do Until Then

Upgrade to 8.23.0 or apply the fix commit to a local build. curl's machine-readable advisory also lists fixed versions on three older branches, and the project said it would ship updated Rock-solid curl releases, its long-term-support line for customers with support contracts, in step with 8.23.0:

  • curl and libcurl 8.12.0 through 8.22.0: upgrade to 8.23.0
  • 8.14.x branch: 8.14.3
  • 8.16.x branch: 8.16.2
  • 8.20.x branch: 8.20.2
  • Debian 13 (trixie): 8.14.1-2+deb13u7 through DSA-6558-1, per Debian's tracker. Debian 12 (bookworm) does not carry the vulnerable code.

The release fixes 24 CVEs in all. The other 23 are rated Low.

If you cannot update yet, curl's advice is not to use HTTP/2. The --http1.1 option asks the tool for HTTP/1.1, and applications set CURLOPT_HTTP_VERSION to CURL_HTTP_VERSION_1_1. curl's documentation calls that setting a request, because an existing connection on another version may be reused.

HTTP/2 support in libcurl is a build option. A build without it cannot negotiate HTTP/2, so it cannot reach the upload path the advisory describes.

How a Hostile Server Turns the Bug Into Code Execution

Daniel Stenberg, curl's lead developer, explained the bug in a post published with the release, and the public report lays out the code path. HTTP/2 carries several transfers over one connection, and libcurl tracks each transfer with an object it calls an easy handle.

During an upload, the server stalls the transfer by setting the HTTP/2 window to zero, returning part of the response, and then resetting the stream while keeping the connection open. curl treats the reset as a reason to retry.

In cleanup, curl first tells the HTTP/2 layer that the transfer is finished, then flushes the rest of the unsent upload into the same connection. With no transfer registered, those leftover bytes are read as a new request. The line pattern the reporter includes in the uploaded file makes them look like request lines. When they do, a new stream is opened that stores a pointer to the easy handle.

The retry completes on a new HTTP/1.1 connection, and the application frees the handle. The old connection still holds the pointer and uses it when the server sends a frame on that stream, which can happen as the program exits.

In the reporter's exploit, data the server sends lands in the memory the freed handle had used. A request that goes out leaks local addresses, which the server needs to defeat address space layout randomization (ASLR). A function pointer in that memory is overwritten with bytes from the server, and curl then calls it.

Code execution needs the attacker to know the target's exact curl version, architecture, libc allocator and heap layout, to keep two parallel transfers on the right timing, and to fit the payload into about 23 bytes, according to curl's advisory. "The most likely outcome of an attempted attack is rather just a crash," Stenberg wrote, putting the chance of success as slim. That is why curl graded the flaw High rather than Critical.

curl uses four severity levels and publishes no CVSS score. The National Vulnerability Database had not analyzed the record as of October 14.

The fix is a six-line reorder in lib/multi.c by Stefan Eissing. The HTTP/2 layer now gives up its references to the handle after the leftover upload data has been flushed, not before.

The report reached curl on September 15 through HackerOne, and the security team confirmed it within hours, according to Stenberg. On October 7, the project pre-announced a High-severity fix for the next release, shortening its cycle from eight weeks to six.

curl credits the finding to "Luna with Claude, Anthropic." Stenberg names the reporter as Luna Tong of Anthropic, says the finding came through the company's new OSS Scanner, and presumes its AI models were involved.

Anthropic opened OSS Scanner on October 8 as an opt-in service that scans enrolled open-source projects with its models and emails the results without human review, each report with a reproducer and, where available, a candidate patch. The curl report came three weeks before that public launch. Anthropic's launch post quoted Stenberg saying the scanner had turned up "one of the worst curl vulnerabilities reported in the last few years," without naming one.

The same maintainer wrote in July 2025 that about a fifth of curl's security submissions that year were what he called AI slop, and that only about one in twenty had proved genuine.

curl has spent several years reducing the number of internal pointers to handles in favor of identifiers it looks up when needed, Stenberg wrote, and that is no guarantee against another use-after-free. curl calls the bug a mistake that a memory-safe language would likely have avoided, and the project does not plan to rewrite curl in one.

item.title: CISA Urges Immediate Ivanti Connect Secure Updates as Honeypots Log 105 Exploit Attempts (2026)
item.description:
The U.S. Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency (CISA) on Tuesday urged organizations to take steps to immediately update their Ivanti Connect Secure (ICS) appliances and deployments to the latest version following the disclosure of an actively exploited vulnerability.

The security flaw, tracked as CVE-2026-104935 (CVSS score: 8.6), is a case of authentication bypass impacting ICS versions 25.1.1.1 and prior, 25.1.2.2 and prior, and 22.8R2.4 and prior that could allow a remote unauthenticated attacker to execute arbitrary commands.

"CISA is aware of cyber threat actors exploiting this zero-day authentication bypass vulnerability, which allows remote, unauthenticated execution of arbitrary commands, to conduct credential theft and data exfiltration," the agency said. 

The agency has since added the flaw to its Known Exploited Vulnerabilities (KEV) catalog, requiring Federal Civilian Executive Branch (FCEB) agencies to apply the fixes by October 16, 2026.

CISA is also recommending that customers of affected ICS deployments review Ivanti's Connect Secure Upgrade and Migration Compatibility Guide for patching guidance, cautioning that version 22.8 reaches end-of-life on January 31, 2027.

"Organizations seeking to determine whether they were compromised will need to conduct network and memory forensics to identify evidence of exploitation," it added.

In the event a compromise is detected, CISA is advising organizations to implement the following actions -

  • Create a backup of the appliance configuration.
  • Conduct a factory reset and upgrade the appliance to the latest version. 
  • For cloud and virtual systems, rebuild the virtual instance and upgrade to the latest version. 
  • Restore the appliance configuration from the backup created in step 1. 
  • Reset passwords for all accounts, including domain, administrator, and local accounts. Revoke and reissue stored certificates; reset stored API keys and license server credentials. 

The development comes as Previdian disclosed that it has observed 105 exploitation attempts targeting its honeypot sensors as of October 14, 2026. The attack attempts have originated from 50 unique IP addresses geolocated to Singapore and the U.S. Some of the observed IP addresses are listed below -

  • 216.73.160[.]59
  • 216.73.160[.]61
  • 216.73.160[.]210
  • 45.8.19[.]111

According to Previdian founder and CEO, Ryan Dewhurst, threat actors are using the X-DSCGI-PATH header to reach an internal CGI handler and upload Perl scripts dressed up as ZIP files. The scripts return unique markers that determine whether remote code execution has succeeded.

"We're seeing coordinated attempts to exploit this Ivanti vulnerability, but the payloads captured so far are primarily testing for code execution rather than deploying malware, or compromising the device," Dewhurst told The Hacker News. "However, full weaponized exploitation is likely to follow in the coming hours and days."

In a separate report, Volexity said it first observed the exploitation of CVE-2026-104935 on October 3, 2026, with a previously undocumented threat actor dubbed UTA0576 leveraging it in conjunction with a privilege escalation vulnerability to achieve unauthenticated root-level code execution. UTA0576 is assessed to be driven by criminal motives rather than espionage.

Following successful exploitation, the threat actor is said to have engaged in broad post-exploitation actions, including extracting credentials stored on the ICS VPN appliance, exfiltrating limited Active Directory metadata, deploying a Kerberos tool capable of Kerberoast attacks and credential testing, conducting host reconnaissance, LDAP packet capture, and dropping a Python LDAP tool to search for administrator passwords and BitLocker recovery keys.

"The recovered payloads demonstrate deliberate efforts to conceal malicious activity through selective log modification, removal of temporary execution artifacts, and restoration of altered system state," Volexity researchers Charlie Gardner, Sean Koessel, and Steven Adair said.

"UTA0576 deployed no malware or web shell. Instead, the threat actor re-exploited the device for every command it ran and tampered with logs to cover its tracks, evading Ivanti's Integrity Checker Tool."

Threat intelligence company Defused Cyber has also confirmed active exploitation, stating its decoys "caught pre-disclosure exploitation we assess as CVE-2026-104935" in the wild starting October 1, 2026.

"The root cause of the vulnerability is incredibly simple, with a single request containing a specially crafted 'X-DSCGI-PATH' header being all that is needed to bypass authentication and access sensitive functionality that otherwise should be restricted," Yordan Ganchev, principal threat intelligence specialist at watchTowr, said.

"Ivanti Connect Secure has long been a popular target for attackers, including ransomware gangs, and joins 14 other Ivanti Connect Secure / Pulse Connect Secure vulnerabilities on the CISA KEV list. Given the history, we expect exploitation to move incredibly quickly from targeted attacks to indiscriminate mass exploitation."

It's essential that organizations running ICS patch immediately and investigate their appliances for signs of compromise, including identifying any inbound requests featuring an "X-DSCGI-PATH" header.
